newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA SEMIS-Moody's bears WA, Vic gifts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA SEMIS-Moody's bears WA, Vic gifts.

text.p: *The Victorian and Western Australian states were given a Christmas bonus on Monday with Moody's upgrade of their domestic currency denominated bonds.
Australian debt markets have been fairly subdued in the past week in the run-up to the Christmas holiday and semis have been no exception.
However, the Victorian and Western Australian states were given a bonus with Moody's Investor Services upgrading their domestic currency denominated bonds.

The timing of the news was a surprise to the market, and in normal trading conditions there may have been more of a price reaction, although traders said that both moves had been anticipated, particularly in the case of Victoria.
Moody's upgraded Victoria to Aa1 from Aa2, bringing it into line with the AA-plus rating from Standard Poor's announced in September.

Meanwhile, Western Australia (WA) was raised to Aaa from Aa1, joining the New South Wales and Queensland states as holders of Moody's highest credit rating, and reflects its improved financial performance and a significant reduction in net debt.

"(The) upgrade represents a reward for the Court government who have addressed the fiscal damage caused by the previous government's excessive spending," said Louise Pollard, analyst at Nomura Research Australia.
Premier Richard Court's Liberal/National coalition government was re-elected on December 14.

"The positive economic outlook for Western Australia's large resource sector and a continuation of the sound economic management policies of the government will place Western Australia in a strong position to maintaining its Aaa rating over the foreseeable future," Pollard added.
WA lost its Aaa rating in 1992 due to rising debt and a deteriorating budget.
Moody's said the upgrading of Victoria reflects the sharp improvement in the state's debt profile as well as continued favourable developments in its budget position.

The rating agency added that the government's victory in the March elections gave it a mandate to carry on with reform, which has seen a A$9.5 billion fall in net debt during 1995/96 following large scale privatisations.
